interview_metadata.name: Tucker Baker
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Alright, well, I was born and raised right here in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho. My folks are pretty regular people — my dad worked construction most of his life, my mom did some bookkeeping part-time and mostly kept the house running for me and my younger sister. Growing up I was outside all the time. We had this little patch of woods behind the house and I'd disappear in there for hours building forts or messing around with my dad's tools. Fishing on Lake Coeur d'Alene was a Saturday thing for as long as I can remember. School was kind of a mixed bag for me. I did fine in elementary, but middle school is where I started losing interest. I was way more into shop class and anything I could do with my hands than sitting in algebra. By the time I hit high school I was just kind of skating by. I dropped out partway through my senior year — eleventh grade really, technically. My dad got hurt on a job and money got tight, and a buddy's uncle had an opening at the fab shop, so I started working there full-time. That's where I still am now, about four years in. I weld, I read blueprints, I run the spot welder, do some CNC setup. Relationship-wise, I've dated here and there but nothing serious that stuck. Never been married, no kids. Still live in town, share a place with a couple roommates. I guess the big stuff in my life so far has been losing my grandpa about three years ago — that hit me harder than I expected — and getting this job and figuring out I'm actually pretty good at it. I'm working on getting my GED right now and looking at a production tech program. That's pretty much me in a nutshell.

follow_ups.question: What was your grandpa like, and what made losing him hit so hard?
follow_ups.response: He was my mom's dad. Quiet guy, big hands, smelled like motor oil and pipe tobacco. He's the one who taught me how to use a wrench and gave me that '98 Honda motorcycle I'm still restoring. After my dad got hurt and was laid up, my grandpa was kind of the steady one. He died of a heart attack in his garage. I think it hit me because I didn't get to say anything, you know? I went up there the next weekend like I always did and he was just gone.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep in touch with your sister?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, Hannah. She's nineteen, lives with my folks still, doing some classes at North Idaho College. We text a lot, get dinner on Sundays at my mom's place most weeks. She's the smart one in the family, going to be a nurse.

follow_ups.question: When you dropped out, was that hard on your folks?
follow_ups.response: Mom was upset, not gonna lie. She cried about it. My dad was quieter — I think he understood because we needed the money, but he made me promise I'd get my GED someday. I'm finally making good on that, so.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, I think the big one was about a year after I started at the shop. I'd been goofing off some, calling in once in a while, not really taking it seriously. My foreman, guy named Dale, sat me down one afternoon and just said straight out, 'Tucker, you can keep messing around and I'll have to let you go, or you can lock in and I'll teach you stuff that'll actually set you up.' I went home that night kind of mad at first, but I thought about it a lot. I could've just quit and bummed around or chased another easy job, but something about him taking the time to say it instead of just firing me made me want to prove him right. After that I started showing up early, asking him questions, picking up the welding side. That was the moment I think I went from being a kid with a job to actually having a trade.

follow_ups.question: Is Dale still your foreman?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, he is. He's like fifty-something, been there twenty-five years. We grab coffee at the gas station before shift sometimes. Good guy.

follow_ups.question: What do you think would've happened if he'd just fired you instead?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? I probably would've ended up working at one of the warehouses out by the highway, or doing landscaping for cash. Nothing wrong with that but I wouldn't have a real skill. I think I would've drifted for a while.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was a real choice. I remember sitting on my bed that night staring at the ceiling making up my mind. I don't make a lot of dramatic decisions, but that one I did on purpose.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually trust your gut or think things through?
follow_ups.response: Think things through. I'm slow about decisions. Drives some people nuts but I'd rather be sure.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: I mean, Dale was that person, basically. Maybe the high school could've done more before I dropped out — nobody really asked why I was checking out. But once I was working, it really came down to having one guy who gave a damn.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone at school try to keep you from leaving?
follow_ups.response: Counselor sent me a couple emails. That was about it. Wasn't really her fault, she had like four hundred kids.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: No partner right now, no kids. Family-wise, my mom and dad are still here in town — they live in the same house I grew up in over off 15th Street. My mom, Lisa, she's a sweetheart, calls me every Sunday morning whether I want her to or not. My dad, Ron, he's recovering from another back surgery he had last fall, so he's been at the house more. We get along but we're both kind of quiet. My sister Hannah I already mentioned. Then there's my grandma on my mom's side, Patricia, she's in an assisted living place over in Hayden. I try to get out there once or twice a month and bring her a cinnamon roll from this bakery she likes. On my dad's side I've got an uncle in Spokane who I see maybe twice a year, and cousins scattered around. We're not super tight but we're not estranged either. Family's important to me but we're not the type that's hugging all the time. It's more like, we show up when somebody needs help moving or their car breaks down.

follow_ups.question: What's the bakery your grandma likes?
follow_ups.response: Bakery by the Lake. Their cinnamon rolls are the size of your hand. She'll only eat half but she lights up when I show up with the box.

follow_ups.question: Have you been dating anyone recently?
follow_ups.response: Went out with a girl a couple times last winter, didn't really go anywhere. I'm not in a rush. Coeur d'Alene's a small enough town that you kind of know everybody already.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: That's pretty much it for immediate. My mom's brother passed when I was a kid, so it's mostly just the folks, Hannah, and my grandma.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember much about your uncle?
follow_ups.response: Not really, I was maybe six when he passed. Car accident. There's pictures of him holding me as a baby.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. My buddy Cody, I've known him since like seventh grade — he works construction now, married with a kid. We fish together pretty much every other weekend in the summer. Then there's Marcus, he's a guy from the shop, he's about thirty, he's kind of taken me under his wing on the welding side. We'll grab a beer after work sometimes. And then there's the hiking club crowd — I go on hikes with the Coeur d'Alene Hiking Club a couple times a month, and there's a handful of regulars I'd call friends, like Jen and her husband Pete who lead a lot of the trips.

follow_ups.question: How'd you end up in the hiking club?
follow_ups.response: Cody's wife signed me up as a joke for my birthday two years ago. Twenty bucks for the year. Joke's on her, I actually love it.

follow_ups.question: What's Cody's kid's name?
follow_ups.response: Little girl, Hazel. She's three. I'm not really an uncle type but I'm trying.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in a rental house off Government Way, sort of north end of Coeur d'Alene. It's a mix of older single-family houses and some duplexes, kind of working-class. Lots of trucks in driveways, people running snowblowers in winter and lawn mowers in summer. There's a little park down the street, a Walmart not too far, and the lake's like a ten-minute drive. My neighbors are mostly older folks who've been there forever and then a few younger renters like me and my roommates. It's pretty quiet. You hear trains sometimes at night. The downtown area is about a fifteen-minute drive south and that's where all the lake stuff and restaurants are — gets busy with tourists in the summer.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors at all?
follow_ups.response: The older couple next door, Hank and Joyce, yeah. I shovel their walk in winter and they bring me cookies at Christmas. It's a good arrangement.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been in that place?
follow_ups.response: About two years. Before that I lived in a basement apartment closer to downtown that flooded twice.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Pretty safe, yeah. I'll walk to the gas station at midnight without thinking about it. There's some property crime once in a while — somebody got into my truck a couple years back and took a multimeter and some change — but it's not a scary place.

follow_ups.question: Do you lock your doors at night?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, but mostly out of habit. My folks didn't growing up.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Mostly upside for me. The downside is rent's gone way up in the last few years because all these California people moved in. Houses I could've bought for one-fifty five years ago are now four hundred grand. Other than that, I love being here. Lake, mountains, the people are mostly decent.

follow_ups.question: Has the price stuff made you think about leaving?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. But everywhere's expensive. And my whole life is here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Two roommates. One's a guy named Brett, he's twenty-four, works at the Toyota dealership in service. We've known each other since high school. The other is Devin, he's twenty-six, he does landscaping in summer and snow plowing in winter. Brett's been there as long as me, two years. Devin moved in about eight months ago when the previous roommate, this guy Kyle, moved to Boise for a girlfriend. We get along pretty well. Each pay our third of rent and utilities, kitchen's a bit of a war zone sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Do you guys hang out outside the house or just kind of coexist?
follow_ups.response: Mix. We'll watch Seahawks games together on Sundays, maybe grill once in a while. But we all do our own thing too. Brett's got a girlfriend so he's gone a lot.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everybody's permanent, on the lease.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Brett's girlfriend Kayla stays over maybe two or three nights a week. Otherwise no.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: Nope, everybody's around.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are pretty locked in. Up at five-thirty, coffee, drive to the shop, on the floor by six-thirty. Work till three-thirty, sometimes overtime till five or six. Get home, shower, eat something, mess around in the garage on the bike or watch TV. Bed by ten usually. Tuesdays and Thursdays I've been doing GED prep online for an hour or two after dinner. Weekends are different — Saturdays I'm usually fishing or hiking, depending on weather and season. Sunday is family dinner at mom's around five, and then I do laundry and prep lunches for the week.

follow_ups.question: What do you bring for lunch usually?
follow_ups.response: Sandwiches, leftovers, sometimes I make a big batch of chili on Sunday and eat that all week.

follow_ups.question: How long's your commute?
follow_ups.response: About fifteen minutes. Shop's just outside town off Highway 95.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm an assembler at a metal fabrication shop. We make custom parts, mostly for industrial equipment, some trailer hitches and racks, some structural stuff for builders. Day shift, six-thirty to three-thirty, Monday through Friday, with overtime offered most weeks. I do blueprint reading, assembly with hand and power tools, spot welding both MIG and TIG, basic CNC setup, and I help with QC. I've been there about four years.

follow_ups.question: Do you do overtime most weeks?
follow_ups.response: Usually a few hours, yeah. Sometimes a Saturday morning if we've got a deadline. The extra money's nice.

follow_ups.question: Which welding do you prefer, MIG or TIG?
follow_ups.response: TIG. Slower, more precise. MIG is fine for production but TIG feels more like a craft.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Couple things. I help my dad around his house with stuff he can't do because of his back — like I mow his lawn April through October, do the gutters, plow the driveway in winter. I check in on my grandma at the assisted living place twice a month. And I volunteer maybe four or five times a year at the community center for cleanups and that food drive they do around Thanksgiving.

follow_ups.question: What's the community center one like?
follow_ups.response: Just a Saturday morning thing. Show up, get assigned to a team, pick up trash along the lake trail or paint over graffiti. Couple hours, free pizza after.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Main thing is starting the GED stuff back in January. Used to be I'd come home and just watch TV or play video games, now I try to do at least an hour twice a week of practice tests. Also been trying to lift weights three mornings a week before work — that's newer, started in March. Less consistent than I'd like but I'm getting there.

follow_ups.question: Where do you lift?
follow_ups.response: Little gym near the shop, twenty bucks a month, real bare-bones. Just dumbbells and a squat rack basically.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: No kids, so doesn't apply to me.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Nothing major. I got pulled over a couple times for speeding, got one ticket and one warning. When my truck got broken into I called the sheriff and a deputy came out, took a report, was decent about it but nothing came of it. That's about it. I've got a couple buddies whose brothers are deputies, so I kind of see them as just regular guys.

follow_ups.question: How fast were you going on the ticket?
follow_ups.response: Seventy-two in a fifty-five on Highway 95. Was late for work. Lesson learned.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Honestly nothing really stands out beyond that. They're just kind of around town, I don't have strong feelings either way.

follow_ups.question: Anyone in your family in law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: No, nobody close.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I've never been arrested. I had a cousin on my dad's side who got picked up for DUI a few years back, did a little time and is supposedly cleaned up now. That's the only one I know of in the family.

follow_ups.question: Are you guys still in touch?
follow_ups.response: Not really. See him at funerals.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in the presidential ones. Voted in 2020 and 2024. The local stuff I skip more often than I should — I voted in one school board election once because my mom told me to. I know that's not great. I should pay more attention to local but it just feels like a lot of homework and I never know who any of these people are.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for in the big ones?
follow_ups.response: Honestly? Mostly gut and what my dad thinks. We talk politics a little. I've never been a sit-down-and-research-it kind of person.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd say I lean conservative but I'm not real loud about it. Working-class North Idaho conservative I guess is the way to put it. I think government should mostly stay out of people's business, I'm pro-Second Amendment because I hunt and a lot of folks around here do, I'm generally for less taxes and regulation on small businesses. But I'm not one of these guys who's super online or angry about it. I think both parties have their head up their butt half the time. On social stuff I'm pretty live-and-let-live — if somebody's gay or whatever, that's their business, not mine. I'm not religious so I don't get worked up about that side of it. I worry about the cost of living more than anything political — like rent and groceries going up, that's the thing that affects me. I think a lot of people in office, both sides, are kind of out of touch with what it's like to actually try to save up to buy a house on a regular wage. I voted for Trump in 2024 honestly more because I liked the economic stuff than because I love the guy personally — he's a lot. But Harris didn't feel like she got us either.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with your friends?
follow_ups.response: Some. Cody and me will, Marcus at work will. We mostly agree which makes it easier. Brett, my roommate, he's more middle-of-the-road and we don't really get into it.

follow_ups.question: Anything you wish your side talked about more?
follow_ups.response: Yeah — trades. I wish there was way more focus on making it easier for people like me to get certifications without going broke. Everybody talks college, college, college. There's millions of us who don't want that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I'd say I've gotten a little less knee-jerk about it as I've gotten older. When I was eighteen, nineteen I'd parrot whatever my dad and his buddies said. Now I'll actually push back on stuff sometimes. Like I think the way some people around here talk about immigrants is just mean and a lot of it doesn't match my own experience — I work next to a guy named Hector who's the best welder I know and he's a citizen now but came up from Mexico. I've gotten more skeptical of really angry people on either side. Probably the biggest shift.

follow_ups.question: What does Hector think when he hears people say that stuff?
follow_ups.response: He's pretty quiet about it. He'll roll his eyes when somebody at the shop says something dumb. I think he's used to it.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat, I'd say. Honestly Coeur d'Alene is almost all white, so it's not like I see it day-to-day. When all that stuff was happening back in 2020 I watched the news and I read about the George Floyd thing and I thought what happened to him was wrong, clearly. I don't agree with all of the protest stuff or the defund-the-police stuff. I think most cops are doing a hard job and some of them are bad and we should weed those out. That's kind of where I land. It didn't change my life but it made me think more about a part of the country I don't really live in.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it at the shop at all?
follow_ups.response: Little bit. Mostly people complained about the protests and Hector and I both kind of stayed out of it.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core thing — that Black folks have gotten a worse shake from police in a lot of places — I believe that's true based on what I've seen on video. I think the harder question is what to do about it, and I don't think the answer is getting rid of police. I think it's accountability, better training, weeding out the bad ones. I don't really have a strong worked-out opinion beyond that. I try not to pretend I know more about the experience than I do.

follow_ups.question: Has your view changed over the years?
follow_ups.response: Got more nuanced. I used to just kind of dismiss it. Now I think there's something to it even if I don't agree with every part.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we're more divided than we should be and a lot of it is people on TV and the internet making money off of getting us mad at each other. In my actual life, with the people I actually meet, race almost never comes up as a problem. So I try not to get too worked up about it. But I know that's partly because of where I live. I don't think we're done with all of it as a country.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mostly keep my thoughts to myself. I'll talk with close friends or family if it comes up. I've never been to a protest of any kind, that's not really my deal.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed. My dad's pretty cynical about the whole thing, thinks it's blown out of proportion. My mom's more sympathetic, she'll watch something on the news and shake her head. Cody doesn't really talk about politics, he'd rather talk about fishing. Most people I know just kind of want it to go back to being about whatever they had going on in their own life.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I'm in pretty good shape overall. Twenty-two, no chronic anything. I tweaked my lower back at the shop a couple months ago lifting something dumb and it bugs me on long days but it's not serious. I've got some hearing damage in my right ear from being around grinders and welders — the shop gives us ear protection but I'm not always great about wearing it. I should get that checked actually. Other than that I'm fine. I eat okay, mostly, I'm outside a lot, I sleep alright.

follow_ups.question: How's your eating actually look on a regular day?
follow_ups.response: Coffee and a granola bar for breakfast, sandwich and chips for lunch, something with meat and potatoes for dinner. Not great but not terrible. I drink way too much Mountain Dew, my one vice.

follow_ups.question: Have you been to a doctor in the last year?
follow_ups.response: Not for a check-up, no. Last time I went was for a sprained ankle two years ago. I should go.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy part is I'm naturally active — my job's on my feet and I'm outdoors a lot off-hours. Hard part is time and money. I've got insurance through work but the deductible's high so going to the doctor for anything not-emergency feels like throwing money away. And cooking healthy stuff after a ten-hour shift is hard when there's a Taco Bell on the way home.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. Sprained ankle two summers ago hiking — twisted it on loose rock and had to limp out three miles. Got an X-ray, nothing broken, off it for two weeks. The back thing this winter I mentioned. Otherwise pretty boring.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Not really for me. The back thing I worked through, took ibuprofen, was fine. Knock on wood. My dad's a different story — his back stuff has kept him from working full time for years.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. My dad's back is the big one — he's had two surgeries, the last one in October. It's stressful for the family because he's in pain a lot and money's tight when he can't work. My grandma's slowing down too, she's eighty-two, dementia's starting to creep in. That weighs on me, especially on my mom because she's the one who deals with it most. I help where I can but I'm not there day to day.

follow_ups.question: How's your mom holding up with all that?
follow_ups.response: She's tough but you can tell it wears her down. I try to call her midweek just to chat, not just on Sundays.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Yeah, for me, I've skipped going to the doctor for stuff that probably wasn't a big deal but I didn't want to pay. The ear thing I mentioned — I've been putting off getting tested for like a year. Dentist too, I haven't been in two years. For my dad it's been a fight with insurance and bills, they had to set up payment plans for the surgery. My mom skipped a colonoscopy she should've had. It's a thing.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really. My mom does some essential oils stuff for headaches and uses elderberry syrup when she gets a cold but that's about as far as it goes. Nothing like acupuncture or anything formal.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I drink, yeah. Not a ton, but a few beers a couple nights a week is normal for me. More on weekends. Maybe six to ten beers across the week on average. I don't smoke cigarettes — tried it a couple times in high school, didn't take. I'll have a cigar once in a while when we're out at the fire pit. After my grandpa died I drank more than usual for a few weeks, but I noticed it and dialed back.

follow_ups.question: What kind of beer?
follow_ups.response: Coors Banquet usually. Sometimes whatever local IPA's on at the bar.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I'll smoke weed once in a while, it's legal across the border in Washington. Maybe once a month, on a weekend night, usually with Cody when his wife's out with her friends. Last time was probably three weeks ago — we shared a joint sitting around his fire pit talking about nothing. I don't take any prescriptions. Ibuprofen when my back hurts.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: For me, employer insurance covers most of what I'd actually need — it's just the deductible that makes me skip things. For my folks, my dad's on disability so he's got Medicare and they've got some supplemental insurance through my mom. Still tons of out-of-pocket. They have a payment plan on the most recent surgery, like a couple hundred a month for the next few years.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm fine with regular vaccines. I got my childhood ones, I get a flu shot most years through work. I did get the original COVID one back in 2021 because my employer pushed it but I haven't done the boosters. Kind of in the middle on it.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Honestly? Mostly my mom — she's a worrier and reads up on health stuff. The shop nurse who comes in once a year. I don't really trust TV news on it either direction. I'll skim stuff online but I don't deep-dive.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Overall pretty good. I'd say steady. There were a few rough patches — when my dad had his October surgery I was kind of stressed and low for a few weeks. And the winter here can be hard, January and February are dark and cold and I don't get outside as much. I felt a little flat through that stretch. But spring's been good. The GED stuff is making me feel like I'm pointed somewhere. I'm not anxious or depressed or anything I'd call serious. I'm a pretty even-keel guy.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get through the winter slump?
follow_ups.response: Honestly just grinding through. I try to do more wood projects in the garage, watch college football, hang out with the roommates more. It passes.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Right around my dad's surgery in October. The day of, I drove my mom to the hospital in Spokane, and we sat in the waiting room for like six hours. I was trying to be the strong one for her but inside I was a wreck. He came out fine but the recovery was harder than they said it would be. I was over at their house every other day for like three weeks. I lost some sleep, lost some weight, didn't really tell anybody I was struggling. Cody finally noticed and dragged me out for wings and that helped.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?

summaries.demographer: Tucker Baker is a 22-year-old white, non-Hispanic, US-born man (DOB 2003-08-14) who has lived his entire life in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho (Q85, Q87, Q88, Q89, Q97). He is never-married with no children, sharing a rental house with two male roommates as a renter rather than homeowner — a household formation pattern typical of his cohort and an exurban region with rising housing costs (Q05, Q08, Q11, Q58, Q84). His educational attainment is 11th grade with no diploma, paired with active GED pursuit and a clear vocational ladder in skilled trades, placing him in the working-class non-credentialed-but-upwardly-mobile manufacturing segment (Q01, Q90, Q91, Q108). His parental household (intact, both parents at age 16, father a residential construction worker now on disability, mother a part-time HVAC-firm bookkeeper) is a textbook lower-middle-class trades family (Q98, Q100-Q107).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Tucker exhibits high time-discount discipline around small savings (~$100/paycheck routine, $3,200 emergency cushion, 4% 401k with 3% match) while remaining loss-averse around medium expenses — he postpones discretionary medical care because of a high-deductible plan even though he could afford it (Q31, Q36, Q61, Q82). He responds strongly to identity-based incentives (foreman Dale's mentorship ultimatum shifted his entire work trajectory) and is deliberative rather than impulsive — explicitly self-describes as slow to decide (Q02, Q03). His consumption mix reveals classic lifecycle-of-tradesman patterns: durable-goods purchases on Facebook Marketplace, side income reinvested in tools and the motorcycle (effectively a savings substitute), and overtime as his primary response to income shocks rather than borrowing (Q48, Q60, Q62, Q81). Risk preferences are moderate: he carries an $8,000 truck loan and a low-balance, paid-off-monthly credit card, avoiding revolving debt (Q63, Q64).
summaries.political_scientist: Tucker is a Republican-leaning independent with weak partisan attachment, voting in presidential elections (Trump 2024) but largely opting out of down-ballot races (Q23, Q24, Q95, Q96). His issue priorities are economic (cost of living, housing affordability, trades policy), Second-Amendment (driven by hunting), and broadly libertarian on social questions; he is notably ambivalent rather than activist on race and Black Lives Matter, with a 'somewhat affected' frame and personal narrative shaped by his Latino coworker Hector (Q24, Q25, Q26, Q27). Institutional trust is low for cable news and partisan media but reasonably intact for local employers, the local sheriff (decent encounters), and informal neighborhood reciprocity networks (Q08, Q20, Q42). His civic style is the classic 'quiet neighbor' — high informal mutual aid (shoveling neighbors' walks, family caregiving, community-center volunteering) paired with low formal political participation (Q08, Q17, Q23, Q29).
summaries.psychologist: Tucker presents as a steady, low-arousal, agreeable-conscientious personality: he self-describes as 'even-keel,' 'calm,' 'slow to decide,' and is consistent in describing emotion regulation through behavioral activation (lifting, garage projects, time outdoors) rather than disclosure or rumination (Q03, Q15, Q43, Q45). His coping style during the high-stress fall 2025 period — losing sleep and weight during his father's surgery recovery, but not disclosing until a friend noticed — suggests internalizing tendencies and stoic masculinity norms typical of his cultural environment, mitigated by a small, reliable male peer network (Q44, Q49). Self-concept is strongly tied to competence (craftsmanship in TIG welding, reliability at work, being someone people can call) and to place attachment to Coeur d'Alene and the surrounding outdoors, which serves as both identity anchor and quasi-spiritual resource (Q16, Q47, Q108, Q109). His motivational architecture is mastery-and-security oriented rather than achievement-and-status oriented: he wants a credential ladder, a small home with a shop, and 'steadiness' rather than wealth or recognition (Q108, Q109).
